questions.question: Which change has the largest increase in entropy of the system? Options: A H2O(s) -> H2O(l); B Hg(l) -> Hg(g); C H2O(l) + HCl(g) -> H3O+(aq) + Cl-(aq); D C(graphite) -> C(diamond).
questions.answer: B - Hg(l) -> Hg(g)
steps: Entropy rises most when a substance changes to a gas, because gas particles have far more positions and motion.
Option B is liquid to gas, the largest entropy increase of the four.
Option A (solid to liquid) gives a smaller increase.
Option C forms ions in solution from a gas, which is an ordering effect, so entropy does not rise greatly.
Option D (graphite to diamond) gives a decrease in entropy because diamond is more ordered.
So B is the answer.

questions.question: The equation for an exothermic reaction is shown, and the question asks which of the options is true. The equation and options are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: B: delta S surroundings is positive
steps: The reaction is exothermic, so delta H is negative (A is false).
Heat released to the surroundings gives delta S surroundings = -delta H / T, which is positive (B is true).
A gas (H2) is produced from solid and aqueous reactants, so delta S system is positive (C is false), and the total entropy change is positive for a feasible reaction (D is false).

questions.question: Potassium bromate(V) decomposes to potassium bromide and oxygen. Using the standard molar entropies in the table, calculate the total entropy change, Stotal, at 298 K.
steps: Delta S surroundings = -delta H / T = -(-67 200 J mol-1) / 298 K = +225.5 J K-1 mol-1 (convert kJ to J).
Delta S total = 508.4 + 225.5 = +733.9, which is +734 J K-1 mol-1 (3 s.f.); it is positive, so the decomposition is feasible.

questions.question: Using the graph of Br- concentration against time (bromate(V) and H+ in large excess), determine the order with respect to bromide ions, showing working on the graph.
questions.answer: First order with respect to bromide ions
steps: The curve is an exponential decay, so a constant half-life shows a first-order reaction.

Draw lines on the graph: [Br-] falls from 0.10 to 0.05 mol dm-3 in about 200 s, then from 0.05 to 0.025 in a further 200 s (at about 400 s), and from 0.025 to 0.0125 in another 200 s (at about 600 s).
The half-life is constant (about 200 s), so the order with respect to Br- is 1.

questions.question: In Experiment 2, the initial concentrations of bromate(V) and H+ are changed while Br- is in large excess. Determine the order with respect to bromate(V) and H+, explaining your working.
questions.answer: BrO3- is first order and H+ is second order
steps: Runs 1 and 2: [BrO3-] doubles from 0.1 to 0.2 with [H+] constant, and the rate doubles (3.6 x 10^-3 to 7.2 x 10^-3), so the reaction is first order in BrO3-.
Run 3 compared with run 1: [BrO3-] is x3 and [H+] is x2, and the rate rises by 4.3 x 10^-2 / 3.6 x 10^-3 = 12 = 3 x 4.
The factor of 3 comes from BrO3-, so the remaining factor of 4 comes from doubling [H+], meaning the order with respect to H+ is 2.

questions.question: Give the overall rate equation for the reaction and include the units of the rate constant.
questions.answer: Rate = k[Br-][BrO3-][H+]^2; units of k: dm9 mol-3 s-1
steps: Orders: Br- first order, BrO3- first order, H+ second order, so rate = k[Br-][BrO3-][H+]^2 (overall order 4).
k = rate / ([Br-][BrO3-][H+]^2), so the units are (mol dm-3 s-1) / (mol dm-3)^4 = dm9 mol-3 s-1.

questions.question: The rate constant for the reaction between a bromoalkane and cyanide ions is measured at five temperatures. Plot ln k against 1/T and use it to determine the activation energy, including the sign and units of the gradient. R = 8.31 J mol-1 K-1.
questions.answer: Gradient is about -1.3 x 10^4 K, so Ea = +110 kJ mol-1 (about 1.1 x 10^2)
steps: Plot ln k (y-axis) against 1/T (x-axis) using the five points (3.33 x 10^-3, -10.20), (3.23 x 10^-3, -8.92), (3.13 x 10^-3, -7.51), (3.03 x 10^-3, -6.21) and (2.93 x 10^-3, -4.93); label both axes and draw a straight line of best fit. The points lie on a line with a negative slope.
From ln k = -Ea/R x 1/T + constant, the gradient = -Ea/R.
Ea = -gradient x R = 1.3 x 10^4 K x 8.31 J mol-1 K-1 = 1.1 x 10^5 J mol-1 = +110 kJ mol-1 (positive; give 2 s.f. as the line is read from a graph).

questions.question: The entropy changes of the surroundings and of the system are given for four reactions P, Q, R and S. Which are thermodynamically feasible? Options: A P only, B P and Q only, C R only, D R and S only.
questions.answer: B: reactions P and Q only
steps: A reaction is feasible if delta S total = delta S surroundings + delta S system is positive.
R: -482 + 65 = -417 and S: -563 - 128 = -691 are both negative, so not feasible.

questions.question: For CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g), deltaH = +178 kJ mol-1, what are the signs of deltaS system and deltaS surroundings? The option list is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: B: delta S system positive and delta S surroundings negative
steps: The reaction makes a gas (CO2) from solids, so the disorder increases and delta S system is positive.
The reaction is endothermic (delta H = +178 kJ mol-1), so delta S surroundings = -delta H / T is negative.

questions.question: Which gas would have the greatest standard molar entropy? Options: A NH3, B H2, C N2, D SO2.
questions.answer: D - SO2
steps: Standard molar entropy increases with molar mass and number of atoms in the molecule.
SO2 has the largest molar mass (64) of the four gases and three atoms per molecule.
H2 has the smallest molar mass, so it has the lowest entropy of the four.
So SO2 has the greatest standard molar entropy, option D.

questions.question: Ammonium nitrate is very soluble in water. What is the best explanation? Options: A all ammonium salts are soluble, B activation energy is very low, C enthalpies of hydration are very exothermic, D deltaS system is positive.
questions.answer: D - the entropy change of the system is positive
steps: Ammonium nitrate is an ionic solid that dissolves to give separate ions in solution.
The ions become more dispersed, so the entropy of the system increases (deltaS positive).
A positive entropy change favours dissolution, even though the process is endothermic.
Option A is only a restatement, B concerns kinetics, and C is not the main reason, so D is the best explanation.

questions.question: What is the standard entropy change of the system, in J K-1 mol-1, for N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3? Options: A -198.8, B -129.9, C +129.9, D +198.8.
steps: Gas moles fall from 4 (1 N2 + 3 H2) to 2 (2 NH3), so entropy of the system decreases; the sign is negative.
This leaves options A and B, so the sign rules out C and D.
Using data book standard entropies (NH3 about 192.8, N2 about 191.6, H2 about 130.7 J K-1 mol-1): 2(192.8) - [191.6 + 3(130.7)] = about -198.
This magnitude matches option A (-198.8 J K-1 mol-1) rather than option B.

questions.question: Which substance has the highest standard molar entropy at 298 K and 1 atm? Options: A CO2, B Cu, C C2H5OH, D H2.
questions.answer: A - carbon dioxide, CO2(g)
steps: Gases have much higher entropy than liquids or solids.
Copper is a metallic solid, so it has low entropy; ethanol is a liquid, so it has lower entropy than any gas here.
Both CO2 and H2 are gases, but CO2 has a larger molar mass and more atoms, so it has the higher standard entropy.
So CO2 is the answer, option A.

questions.question: The standard molar entropy of a substance: A is not affected by state changes or temperature; B only changes with temperature; C only changes with state; D changes with temperature and with state change. Which is correct?
questions.answer: D - it changes both with temperature and with a change of state
steps: Entropy rises as temperature rises, because particles have more energy and motion.
Entropy also rises at a change of state (solid to liquid to gas), because particles become less ordered.
So standard molar entropy changes with both temperature and state, which is option D.

questions.question: In which series does the standard molar entropy of the compounds increase? Options: A CaO(s) < H2O(l) < CO2(g) < SO2(g); B CaO(s) < H2O(l) < SO2(g) < CO2(g); C SO2(g) < CO2(g) < H2O(l) < CaO(s); D CO2(g) < SO2(g) < H2O(l) < CaO(s).
questions.answer: A - CaO(s) < H2O(l) < CO2(g) < SO2(g)
steps: Solids have lower entropy than liquids, which have lower entropy than gases: CaO(s) lowest, H2O(l) next, then the gases.
Options C and D put gases before liquids/solids, so they are wrong.
Between CO2 and SO2 (both gases with three atoms), SO2 has the larger molar mass (64 vs 44), so SO2 has the higher entropy.
So the increasing order is CaO(s) < H2O(l) < CO2(g) < SO2(g), option A.

questions.question: Which sequence shows the elements in order of increasing standard entropy? The four options are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: C: Os(s) < Hg(l) < He(g) < O2(g)
steps: Entropy increases from solid to liquid to gas, so Os(s) is lowest, then Hg(l), then the two gases.
Of the two gases, O2 is a diatomic molecule with more ways of storing energy and a higher standard entropy (205 J K-1 mol-1) than monatomic He (126 J K-1 mol-1), so He < O2.

questions.question: Hydrogen and oxygen do not react until a platinum gauze is added, when the mixture explodes. In the absence of platinum, the mixture is: A kinetically stable and thermodynamically stable; B kinetically stable and thermodynamically unstable; C kinetically unstable and thermodynamically stable; D kinetically unstable and thermodynamically unstable.
questions.answer: B - kinetically stable and thermodynamically unstable
steps: Thermodynamic stability is about the energy of the products relative to the reactants: the reaction is exothermic and feasible, so the mixture is thermodynamically unstable.
Kinetic stability is about the rate: the reaction does not start without a catalyst, so the activation energy is high.
Platinum lowers the activation energy and the reaction proceeds rapidly.
So the mixture is kinetically stable and thermodynamically unstable, option B.

questions.question: Flask P contains argon and flask Q is a vacuum; the tap is opened and the argon fills both flasks. How do the entropy and energy of the system change? The option list is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: C: entropy increases and energy is unchanged
steps: The argon spreads into twice the volume, so there are more ways of arranging the atoms and the entropy of the system increases.
Argon is treated as an ideal gas with no intermolecular forces and no work is done against a vacuum, so the total energy of the gas stays the same.

questions.question: Which graph shows the entropy of a substance as it changes state from solid to liquid to gas? The four graphs are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: D: Graph 4
steps: Entropy rises gradually as the temperature rises within each state, so the lines must slope upwards (Graphs 1 and 2 show flat lines, which is wrong).
There is a sudden jump in entropy at each change of state, and the jump at boiling (liquid to gas) is much larger than at melting (solid to liquid), because a gas is far more disordered.
Graph 3 has the larger jump at the first change of state, so only Graph 4 shows both features correctly.

questions.question: Nitrous oxide, N2O, decomposes to nitrogen and oxygen. Using the standard molecular entropy data (table shown in the figure below), calculate the standard entropy change of the system, with sign and units.
steps: Delta S system = sum S(products) - sum S(reactants) = [S(N2) + 1/2 S(O2)] - S(N2O).
= +74.5 J K-1 mol-1 (positive because 1.5 mol of gas forms from 1 mol).

questions.question: The standard enthalpy change of the forward reaction is -82 kJ mol-1. Calculate the entropy change of the surroundings at 2048 K, with sign and units.
steps: Entropy of surroundings: deltaS(surr) = -deltaH(sys) / T.
deltaH = -82 kJ mol-1 = -82 000 J mol-1, so -deltaH = +82 000 J mol-1.
The value is positive because the reaction is exothermic: heat released to the surroundings increases their entropy.

questions.question: Calculate the total entropy change of the reaction at 2048 K, with sign and units, using your answers to (a)(i) and (a)(ii).
steps: Delta S total = delta S system + delta S surroundings.
The value is positive, so the decomposition is thermodynamically feasible.

questions.question: From the rate graph for the decomposition of nitrous oxide, calculate the activation energy in kJ mol-1, including the value of the gradient.
questions.answer: Gradient about -2.9 x 10^4 K, so Ea about +2.4 x 10^2 kJ mol-1 (240 kJ mol-1)
steps: Draw a large right-angled triangle on the line: for example from (0.00646, -189.1) to (0.00672, -196.6).
Gradient = -Ea / R, so Ea = -(-2.9 x 10^4) x 8.31 = 2.4 x 10^5 J mol-1.
Ea = about +240 kJ mol-1 (accept a range for graph reading, about 230 to 250).

questions.question: Explain whether or not this reaction occurs at 2048 K, considering the values calculated in (a) and (b).
questions.answer: The reaction does occur at 2048 K: delta S total is positive (+114.5 J K-1 mol-1) so it is thermodynamically feasible, and at this very high temperature enough molecules exceed the large activation energy (about 240 kJ mol-1) for the rate to be significant.
steps: Feasibility: delta S total from (a)(iii) is positive (+114.5 J K-1 mol-1), so the decomposition is thermodynamically feasible.
Kinetics: the activation energy is high (about 240 kJ mol-1), but the temperature is very high (2048 K), so a large fraction of molecules have energy greater than Ea and the rate is fast enough.
Both conditions are met, so the reaction occurs.

questions.question: Write the overall equation for the rapid decomposition of hydrogen peroxide catalysed by iodide ions, and state the role of the iodide ions.
questions.answer: 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2; iodide ions are a catalyst (used in step 1 and regenerated in step 2)
steps: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes to water and oxygen: 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2.
Iodide ions appear in the first step as a reactant and are regenerated in the second step.
A species that is used and then regenerated, and does not appear in the overall equation, is a catalyst.
So the iodide ions act as a catalyst, lowering the activation energy.

questions.question: Using the table of rate constants at two temperatures, calculate Ea by a non-graphical method, giving the answer in kJ mol-1 with a sign and an appropriate number of significant figures.
questions.answer: +56.0 kJ mol-1
steps: Convert to kelvin: T1 = 22.0 + 273 = 295 K and T2 = 47.0 + 273 = 320 K.
Write ln k at each temperature: ln k1 = -Ea/(R x 295) + c and ln k2 = -Ea/(R x 320) + c; subtract: ln(k2/k1) = (Ea/R)(1/T1 - 1/T2).

questions.question: Explain the formation of the blue-black colour in the clock reaction and why its appearance is delayed.
questions.answer: Iodine formed is reduced by thiosulfate, so no blue-black colour until all thiosulfate is used up; then iodine reacts with starch
steps: Iodine is formed by the reaction between hydrogen peroxide and iodide ions in acid.
Thiosulfate is added in a fixed amount and reduces the iodine as it forms: I2 + 2S2O3^2- -> 2I- + S4O6^2-.
While thiosulfate is present, iodine is removed as fast as it forms, so no iodine builds up.
When all the thiosulfate has been used, iodine accumulates and forms a blue-black starch-iodine complex.
The delay is the time needed to use up the fixed amount of thiosulfate.

questions.question: Oxidation of thiosulfate by hydrogen peroxide is thermodynamically favourable, but does not take place in the clock reaction. Suggest a reason.
questions.answer: The reaction has a high activation energy, so it is too slow to occur at the conditions used
steps: A reaction can be thermodynamically feasible (deltaG negative) but still have a very slow rate.
The oxidation of thiosulfate by hydrogen peroxide has a high activation energy.
Under the conditions of the clock reaction, very few collisions are energetic enough to react.
So the reaction does not compete measurably with the reduction of iodine by thiosulfate.

questions.question: Which substance has the highest standard molar entropy? Options: A ethane(g), B water(s), C water(l), D water(g).
questions.answer: A - ethane(g)
steps: Gases have higher entropy than liquids and solids, so ethane(g) and water(g) are the candidates.
Ethane has a higher molar mass (30) and more atoms (8) than water (18 g mol-1, 3 atoms).
So ethane(g) has the greatest standard molar entropy, option A.

questions.question: Rhombic and monoclinic sulfur are interchangeable solid forms. The value of deltaStotal is given for the forward reaction. What can be concluded? The direction of the forward reaction is shown in a diagram shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: D: monoclinic sulfur could change into rhombic sulfur but nothing can be deduced about the rate
steps: Delta S total for the forward reaction (rhombic to monoclinic) is negative, so that direction is not feasible.
The reverse reaction (monoclinic to rhombic) therefore has a positive delta S total, so it is feasible.
Thermodynamics says nothing about the rate (the activation energy could be high), so nothing can be said about how quickly it happens.

questions.question: For SiO2(s) + 4Mg(s) -> Mg2Si(s) + 2MgO(s), complete the table indicating the type of bonding in the reactants and products.
questions.answer: SiO2: giant covalent (macromolecular); Mg: metallic; Mg2Si: covalent (given); MgO: ionic
steps: SiO2 is a giant lattice of covalently bonded Si and O atoms.
Mg is a metal, so it has metallic bonding.
MgO is a compound of a metal and a non-metal, so it is ionic (Mg2+ and O2-).

questions.question: The entropy change of the system for Reaction 1 is -43.8 J K-1 mol-1. With reference to the equation, suggest why it is negative.
questions.answer: Five moles of solid react to form three moles of solid, so the disorder decreases
steps: Reactants: SiO2(s) + 4Mg(s) = 5 moles of solid.
Products: Mg2Si(s) + 2MgO(s) = 3 moles of solid.
The number of moles of solids falls, so there are fewer ways to arrange the particles.
Solids have low entropy and there is no gas, so the disorder decreases and deltaS is negative.

questions.question: The enthalpy change for Reaction 1 is -370 kJ mol-1. Calculate the entropy change of the surroundings in J K-1 mol-1 at 23.0 C.
steps: Convert temperature: T = 23.0 + 273 = 296 K.
deltaS(surr) = -deltaH / T = -(-370 000 J mol-1) / 296 K.
deltaS(surr) = +1250 J K-1 mol-1.

questions.question: Calculate the total entropy change, deltaStotal, for Reaction 1 at 23.0 C, to an appropriate number of significant figures in J K-1 mol-1.
steps: deltaStotal = deltaSsystem + deltaSsurroundings.
deltaStotal = -43.8 + 1250 = +1206 J K-1 mol-1.
Give the answer to 3 s.f., since the surroundings term has 3 s.f.: +1.21 x 10^3 J K-1 mol-1.
The positive value means the reaction is feasible at 23.0 C.

questions.question: Reaction 1 does not occur at room temperature because its activation energy is very high. Suggest why the activation energy is very high.
questions.answer: Strong covalent Si-O bonds in SiO2 must be broken, and the reaction is between solids with few points of contact
steps: SiO2 is a giant covalent structure with very strong Si-O bonds.
These strong bonds need a large amount of energy to break before the reaction can start.
Both reactants are solids, so there are few points of contact for collisions to occur.
Together these make the activation energy very high, so few collisions are successful at room temperature.

questions.question: Write an equation for the reaction of magnesium silicide, Mg2Si, with hydrochloric acid to form silane, SiH4, and magnesium chloride. State symbols are not required.
questions.answer: Mg2Si + 4HCl -> 2MgCl2 + SiH4
steps: Mg2Si gives 2 Mg atoms and 1 Si atom.
2 MgCl2 use 2 Mg and 4 Cl, so 4 HCl are needed.
SiH4 accounts for the Si and the 4 H atoms from the 4 HCl.
Balanced equation: Mg2Si + 4HCl -> 2MgCl2 + SiH4.

questions.question: Silane, SiH4, has a molecular structure. Complete the table giving the shape of a SiH4 molecule and its bond angle.
questions.answer: Tetrahedral; H-Si-H bond angle 109.5 degrees
steps: Silicon has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs of electrons around it.
The four pairs repel equally, so they arrange tetrahedrally (VSEPR).
The molecular shape is tetrahedral.
The H-Si-H bond angle is 109.5 degrees.

questions.topic: Entropy Change Of System For Combustion
questions.question: Calculate the entropy change of the system, in J K-1 mol-1, for SiH4(g) + 2O2(g) -> SiO2(s) + 2H2O(l), using the entropy data shown.
steps: Reaction 2: SiH4(g) + 2O2(g) -> SiO2(s) + 2H2O(l).
Sum S(products) = 41.8 + 2 x 69.9 = 181.6 J K-1 mol-1.
Sum S(reactants) = 204.5 + 2 x 205.0 = 614.5 J K-1 mol-1.
Delta S system = 181.6 - 614.5 = -432.9 J K-1 mol-1 (negative because 3 mol of gas become liquid and solid).

questions.question: State why the entropy change of the surroundings for silane combustion is highly positive, in terms of the bond strengths of the reactants and products.
questions.answer: The products form stronger bonds (Si-O and O-H) than the bonds broken in the reactants (Si-H and O=O), so a large amount of energy is released to the surroundings
steps: The reaction is strongly exothermic, so a large amount of energy is released to the surroundings.
Bonds broken in the reactants (Si-H and O=O) are weaker than the bonds formed in the products (Si-O and O-H).
The energy released is therefore large, which gives a large positive entropy change of the surroundings.

questions.question: The equations for three reactions involving hydrogen (J, K, L) are shown in a diagram shown in the figure below. What is the order of increasing standard entropy change of the system? Options: A J, K, L; B K, L, J; C K, J, L; D L, K, J.
questions.answer: C: K, J, L
steps: Count the change in moles of gas: J goes from 4 mol of gas to 2 mol of gas (decrease of 2 mol of gas).
K goes from 3 mol of gas to 0 mol of gas (a liquid forms), the largest decrease in disorder, so it has the most negative delta S.
L goes from 1 mol of gas (plus a solid) to 2 mol of gas, so the entropy increases and delta S is positive.
Increasing order of delta S system: K (most negative), then J, then L.

questions.question: What are the signs of the entropy changes at 373 K when water vapour condenses? The option list is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: C: delta S system negative, delta S surroundings positive
steps: Gas condensing to liquid becomes more ordered, so delta S system is negative.
Condensation releases heat (it is exothermic) to the surroundings, so delta S surroundings = -delta H / T is positive.

questions.topic: Entropy Change Of Methane Steam Reaction
questions.question: Methane reacts with steam to form carbon dioxide and hydrogen. Using the standard molar entropies in the table (shown in the figure below), find the entropy change for the reaction. Options: A -174, B -30, C +30, D +174.
questions.answer: D: +174 J K-1 mol-1
steps: Delta S = sum S(products) - sum S(reactants).

questions.question: Some thermodynamic information is given for four reactions W, X, Y and Z at 298 K. Which are feasible? Options: A X only, B W and X only, C Y only, D W and Z only.
questions.answer: B: W and X only
steps: A reaction is feasible when delta S total > 0, which means T delta S system > delta H (delta G = delta H - T delta S system < 0).
W: delta H is negative and more negative than T delta S system, so delta H < T delta S system: feasible.
X: delta H negative and T delta S system positive: always feasible.
Y: T delta S system is positive but smaller than delta H, so T delta S system < delta H: not feasible. Z: delta H positive and T delta S system negative: never feasible.

questions.question: Which pair of values will always give a thermodynamically feasible reaction? The option list is shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: C: entropy change of the system positive and enthalpy change negative
steps: A reaction is feasible when delta S total = delta S system - delta H / T is positive.
If delta S system is positive and delta H is negative, both terms are positive, so delta S total is positive at every temperature.
The other combinations give a negative term that can outweigh the other at some temperatures.

questions.question: Which substance would be expected to have the greatest standard molar entropy? Options: A FeO, B FeS, C FeCl2, D FeCl3.
questions.answer: D - FeCl3
steps: All four are solids, so the choice depends on the complexity of the formula.
Standard molar entropy increases with the number of atoms per formula unit and the molar mass.
FeCl3 has the most atoms per formula unit (4) and the largest molar mass of the four.
So FeCl3 is expected to have the greatest standard molar entropy, option D.

questions.question: Which has the greatest molar entropy? Options: A Hg(l), B H2O(l), C NO(g), D NO2(g).
questions.answer: D - NO2(g)
steps: Gases have much higher molar entropy than liquids, so C and D are the candidates over A and B.
NO2 has a larger molar mass (46) and more atoms (3) than NO (30 g mol-1, 2 atoms).
So NO2(g) has the greatest molar entropy, option D.
